We introduced a microscopic theory of quasiparticle scattering by magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces onto which Majorana fermions emerge. Employing the relativistic self-consistent Born-Oppenheimer approximation to model the Yukawa--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) state, we specifically addressed an Mn adatom and Mn$_{2}$, Mn$_{3}$, Mn$_{4}$ clusters on Nb(110). Our calculations reveal that magnetic splitting arises predominantly from deep in-site orbitals, whereas superconducting gap states mainly stem from in-site orbitals with strong hybridization to conduction electrons. Furthermore, the computed YSR spectral shapes align well with experimental data, and the predicted magnetic and non-magnetic ground states for the Mn$_{2}$ and Mn$_{3}$ clusters match their corresponding experimental configurations. Finally, we determined the binding energies of low-lying YSR excited states for these clusters.

Deriving sufficient training data for every class within the medical image segmentation domain remains a significant challenge. Consequently, there is an urgent need for methods capable of identifying and isolating outlier samples, whether they result from noise, mislabeling, or previously unseen classes. This paper introduces a two-stage approach for skin cancer image segmentation that incorporates an anomaly detection mechanism to capture and separate potential outliers without discarding them. The first stage involves a novel method to detect anomalies, while the second utilizes a deep learning model trained on cleaned data to perform precise segmentation. Evaluations were conducted across three public skin cancer image datasets: ISIC 2017, PH2, and PH1. Results indicate that for ISIC 2017, the proposed anomaly detection method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques by a margin of 1.11% in Mean Class Recall for the "Outlier" class, and the subsequent skin cancer segmentation method achieves a 0.84 improvement in Mean Pixel Recalled. Similarly, when applied to the PH2 and PH1 datasets, the segmentation algorithm demonstrated performance gains compared to a baseline model trained on the same cleaned data. Furthermore, both the anomaly detection and segmentation approaches effectively generalized to the ISIC 2017 dataset, which was not used during training. The validity of the isolated outliers was further confirmed through visual analysis by a dermatologist and automated clustering. Ultimately, this study presents an automatic anomaly detection and segmentation framework for skin cancer image segmentation, with the underlying code available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1003/Anomaly_Detection_and_Segmentation_for_Medical_Images.

This study addresses the inverse problem of a structural acoustic interaction, aiming to reconstruct the back shape of a vibrating plate from the radiation captured by an array of acoustic sensors. While this scenario represents a classic ill-posed issue, the approach adopted here—rooted in operational calculus—avoids traditional regularization techniques. Instead, the method relies on a mathematical model based on fractional derivatives of order strictly less than one. The core objective is to demonstrate that this framework yields a reliable reconstruction without requiring regularization. Additionally, the paper outlines a strategy to extend this method to scenarios involving higher-order ill-posedness. Finally, the work confirms that the fractional derivative model remains valid even when the ill-posedness is high, provided the measurement bandwidth is sufficiently narrow. These findings are particularly significant for applications in active noise control, offering a practical solution to shape reconstruction that bypasses the usual limitations associated with regularization.

We introduce the simplest non-minimal scoto-seesaw model featuring a minimal dark sector, where the dark matter candidate is a singlet WIMP. Using the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO framework, we developed a dedicated workflow for Monte Carlo simulation of workshop-style simple processes, followed by analysis with both simple and sophisticated detectors. This automated approach enables the rapid exploration of extensive phenomenological scenarios, which would otherwise require extensive manual efforts. Within this model, we examine mass matrix structures, dark matter freeze-out mechanisms, production and detection mechanisms at colliders, and vacuum stability. Our results demonstrate that achieving a non-minimal type-I seesaw scale of approximately 10 TeV through mixed neutrino oscillations demands a singlet seesaw scale of at least 100 TeV to close the relevant neutrino mass gap. At tree level, maintaining vacuum stability at such high scales necessitates non-minimal quartic couplings; however, we confirm that including one-loop corrections allows for stability with minimal quartics. Collider phenomenology at the LHC and future 100 TeV proton-proton colliders is ideally suited for investigating this model's parameter space. We present detailed event spectrum results for specific collider processes and highlight a novel, testable signature at 14 TeV proton-proton colliders: the $W$-like resonance signature ($q\bar{b}\rightarrow\tilde{W}^{+}\rightarrow\ell^{+}N_{1}^{0}\rightarrow\ell^{+}j j\chi_{1}^{0}$). Furthermore, we report on simple strategies to verify the presence of this exotic signature at a 100 TeV proton-proton collider. Finally, we provide a comprehensive summary of our findings regarding this model's physics.
